title: Chess Patterns and Planning: Common Checkmates
subject: thinking

sections.body: Strong players recognise patterns. When you have seen a checkmate pattern a few times, you spot it in a game within seconds. Here are some common ones.

BACK-RANK MATE: the enemy king is stuck on its first row behind its own pawns. A rook or queen that reaches that row gives check, and the king cannot escape. The fix, if you are the one in danger, is to make a little escape square for your king with a pawn move such as h3.

SMOTHERED MATE: the king is surrounded by its own pieces, so it has no squares. A knight gives check, and because a knight's check cannot be blocked, it is mate. It often ends with the king in a corner.
QUEEN AND KING MATE: with the queen protected by your king, she can give check right next to the enemy king, which cannot capture her.

Planning matters as much as patterns. Before every move ask three questions: What did my opponent's last move threaten? What are my pieces and my opponent's king doing? Which move improves my position or makes a threat without leaving a piece undefended?
Look at the three checkmate puzzles in the app. For each, write down the pattern name and what trapped the king.
Naming the pattern is a lasting skill: it turns puzzles into recognition. The mate-in-one puzzles in the app use these patterns, and the explanation after each one names it.

quiz.q: A black king on g8 sits behind pawns on f7, g7 and h7. A white rook gives check on the back row and cannot be blocked. What is this pattern?
hints: Where is the king, and what is stopping it from stepping forward?
Its own pawns trap it on its back row.
Example: a king trapped in a corner by its own rook and pawns, and mated by a knight, is a different pattern. Name the pattern that uses a rook on the back row.
quiz.explain: The king's own pawns shut it in on the back rank, and the rook gives check along that rank: a back-rank mate.

quiz.q: A king in the corner is surrounded by its own rook and pawns. A white knight gives check, and no piece can capture it. Which pattern is this?
hints: Look at what stops the king moving.
The king is smothered by its own pieces.
Example: with pawns in front and a rook beside it, the king has no free squares. Name the mate where a knight delivers the check.
quiz.explain: The king cannot move because its own pieces fill the squares around it, and the knight's check cannot be blocked. This is a smothered mate.

quiz.q: Before you move, which question is the most useful habit?
options: What did my opponent's last move threaten?
Which piece have I not moved yet in this game so far?
Can I move my queen to the centre of the board?
hints: Good players check for danger first.
A move that ignores your opponent's threat can lose a piece.
Example: if your opponent moved a knight next to your queen, the first thing to notice is that the queen may be attacked. Pick the question that looks for that kind of danger.
quiz.explain: Checking what your opponent just threatened stops you walking into tactics. It is the best habit in chess.
